<reason>PRO built a clean, durable decision rule: the status quo guarantees destruction every night, while a mandate only needs to redirect some fraction of that certain loss to beat it. CON's operational objections (compliance burden, liability, "form not a table") and mechanism arguments (upstream leakage, hidden waste) were rhetorically sharp and creative, but they only ever established that the mandate is costly or imperfect, not that it produces net harm exceeding the status quo's guaranteed waste. CON's closing move — claiming the "successful" donation nights were already happening voluntarily and shouldn't be credited to the law — contradicts CON's own earlier acceptance that stores currently treat destruction as the frictionless default with no donation plan, creating an internal inconsistency PRO's asymmetry framing exposed without CON fully resolving it. PRO also answered pressure questions directly (A1/A2 format) with a concrete standard for "failure" and used ordinary-knowledge grounding (Good Samaritan laws) to blunt the liability objection, while CON's strongest counters remained speculative mechanisms asserted with confidence but never shown to outweigh certain status-quo destruction. The debate was close and both sides executed the format well, but PRO's core comparison was simpler, more resilient to the pressure exchange, and easier for a judge to apply as a decision rule.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing use of CON's own "dumpster remains on the nights that matter" [B4.7] to argue the converse — that on other nights the mandate succeeds — forced CON into an unsupported and internally inconsistent final move (crediting pre-existing voluntary donation for successes while denying the mandate's own default-flip mechanism established earlier and never rebutted).</best_rebuttal>
